report:
**Conclusion:** Your sister is *partly* right: probiotics **may modestly lower blood sugar on average** in people with type 2 diabetes, but the evidence is inconsistent and not strong enough to regard them as a proven diabetes treatment.

Meta-analyses of randomized trials report small reductions in fasting glucose and HbA1c. A 2024 review estimated an HbA1c reduction of **0.33 percentage points** (95% CI −0.59 to −0.07)—a potentially real but usually modest change. [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/39114293/) Earlier analyses have found similar benefits (e.g., HbA1c −0.24 percentage points and fasting glucose −0.44 mmol/L), while other analyses found **no significant HbA1c improvement**. [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31952517/?dopt=Abstract) [PubMed](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31691101/)

Why uncertainty remains: trials use different bacterial strains, doses, foods versus supplements, durations, baseline glucose levels, and diabetes medications; many are short and small. A systematic review identified 21 probiotic-versus-control trials, most allowing participants to continue usual diabetes treatment and diet—so probiotics’ independent effect is difficult to isolate. [PMC](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8166562/)

**Practical takeaway:** A probiotic food or supplement might be a reasonable *adjunct* if her clinician agrees, but it should not replace prescribed medication, nutrition changes, activity, weight management, or glucose monitoring. Current expert reference guidance says evidence is insufficient to recommend probiotics specifically for glycemic control. [Endotext](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK279012/)
